newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Failure to reform EU would be catastrophic - Santer.
newsitem.headline: Failure to reform EU would be catastrophic - Santer.

text.p: European Commission President Jacques Santer said on Monday that a rejection of the Amsterdam treaty on EU institutional reform would be catastrophic for both the internal cohesion and the planned enlargement of the 15-nation group.

Plans to expand the European Union depended on a successful conclusion to the EU's Intergovernmental Conference (IGC) in Amsterdam in June, Santer said in a lecture on European integration entitled "A message for the sceptics."

"Rejection of the (Amsterdam) treaty would be catastrophic. Not only for the inner cohesion of the Union - which is reason enough - but also for tackling successfully a commitment... which may turn out to be the biggest challenge the Union has ever had to face. I refer of course to enlargement," he said.
Santer urged Euro-sceptics not to derail progress and to be as constructive as possible.

"We have started to move forward again. So there is no point at all in keeping our feet on the brakes - indeed it is even dangerous. Be constructive, not destructive. That is my message for the sceptics - wherever in Europe," he said.
He said the Amsterdam Treaty should reform EU institutions in a way which made decision-making more efficient and which raised confidence among European citizens.
Efficiency, Santer said, demanded the end of unanimous decision-making, particularly in an enlarged European Union.
"Unanimity should be replaced as much as possible by majority decisions....No one wants gridlock," he said.
But he conceded there might still be scope for countries to adopt decisions at different speeds, although he hoped such opt-outs would be used only in exceptional circumstances.
"We need the instrument of flexibility, or to use a better expression: enhanced cooperation," he said.
Decision-making procedures also had to be streamlined: "We now have 23 such procedures which only experts can comprehend. Three is enough," he said.
To appease Europe's citizens, it was vital to address their main concerns, among them unemployment of around 18 million, he said.
"I am in favour of introducing into the Treaty a new employment chapter as well as the - now separate - social protocol," he said.
The aim of such a chapter was to focus the minds of governments and stimulate negotiations, Santer said.
He also said the Union must be able to speak with one voice on political matters.
"Progressively, we must build a military capability - without it, credibility will be weak," he said.
Credibility and confidence, he said, extended to the euro, the single European currency due to be launched in 1999.

"Let's stop conjuring ghosts of defeat.... Citizens should be informed about the changes to come, about the advantages which the euro will hold for them as consumers, savers, workers or tourists," Santer said.
